items.title: Consensus Statements on the Clinical Practice for Patients With Fontan-Associated Liver Disease.
items.abstract: The Fontan procedure has been transformative for patients with univentricular physiology. By using a single ventricle as the systemic pump and relying on passive venous return to drive pulmonary circulation, Fontan circulation alleviates cyanosis and heart failure, allowing children to engage in normal activities during school and adolescence. Nevertheless, Fontan circulation is characterized by chronically elevated systemic venous pressure, which leads to systemic venous congestion and long-term multiorgan effects. Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) is now recognized as a major long-term complication. Approximately 50% of patients develop hepatic abnormalities within 10-20 years after surgery, and some progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Despite this risk, strategies to identify individuals at high risk for early HCC and to provide better prognostic information remain limited. This article compiles knowledge from congenital heart disease specialists and hepatologists on FALD, including areas where evidence is limited. By facilitating early diagnosis, structured follow-up, and multidisciplinary management of FALD, this initiative aims to improve outcomes, build a nationwide clinical experience, and ultimately support the development of formal, evidence-based guidelines for FALD management.

items.title: Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation: From Prolapse to Precision Therapy.
items.abstract: Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse affects ≈15 million people globally and is the commonest indication for mitral intervention in high-income countries, but its biology, natural history, and lifetime management are ill defined. This review summarizes current knowledge of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, risk stratification, and lifetime management of degenerative mitral regurgitation, with a focus on areas of uncertainty, recent advances, and emerging research directions. These include translational research focused on determining genetic and cellular drivers of disease progression and mechanistic studies geared to improve detection and prevention of downstream myocardial dysfunction, particularly in high-risk phenotypes, including arrhythmic mitral prolapse. The current landscape of randomized trials and large registries comparing contemporary surgical and transcatheter treatment and strategies to improve patient access to care and outcomes across all patient risk profiles and populations are also discussed.

items.title: Sex-specific challenges and psychosocial adaptation in women with implantable cardioverter defibrillators.
items.abstract: Although cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in women globally, it is underdiagnosed and undertreated. Implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death, but many women report diminished quality of life and avoidance behaviors and present sex-specific challenges postimplantation. Women have higher rates of concern, comorbidities, psychological distress, and anatomic factors that can affect the outcomes of ICD therapy. Women experience more ICD-related complications, psychological distress, and body image concerns, which can adversely affect their quality of life and ICD implant adjustments. Anatomic differences and comorbidities may contribute to these issues. Despite these factors, women remain underrepresented in clinical trials and receive ICD therapy less often than men. Psychosocial interventions such as education, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and support groups have shown promise in improving outcomes, but further research is required to assess their effectiveness. Although current interventions show potential, persistent disparities in utilization and research underscore the need for sex-specific strategies. This article explores sex-specific challenges and outcomes associated with ICD therapy in women, and highlights opportunities for tailored interventions to improve quality of life, sexual health, and well-being.

items.title: Familial Ovarian Teratoma With Neural Tissue Expression and Anti-NMDAR Encephalitis.
items.abstract: Anti-N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is frequently associated with ovarian teratoma. We report an extremely rare parent-child occurrence of teratoma-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis, with pathologic findings and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing. Ovarian teratoma specimens were examined for GluN1 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) by immunohistochemistry, and HLA typing was performed using next-generation sequencing . The mother and daughter developed anti-NMDAR encephalitis at 29 and 12 years of age, respectively, with ovarian teratomas. Both were positive for CSF anti-NMDAR antibodies, and teratomatous neural tissue was GluN1-positive. In addition, the daughter was positive for serum MOG antibody. Early immunotherapy and tumor resection led to favorable neurologic recovery. Recurrent teratomas occurred without encephalitis relapse, and no known high-risk HLA alleles were shared. This extremely rare parent-child occurrence suggests that familial ovarian teratoma with neural tissue expression may predispose individuals to anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Further studies are needed to clarify genetic susceptibility and tumor-related immune mechanisms.

items.title: Quality of Life Benefits Through Prospective Neurotoxicity Assessment in Patients With Cancer: Insights From the NTox-PARTICIPATE Study.
items.abstract: Neurologic adverse events associated with oncological immunotherapies, including CAR T-cell therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors, are becoming increasingly prevalent. The NTox-PARTICIPATE trial was designed to characterize the neurologic effects of CAR T-cell therapy and checkpoint inhibitors (target group) compared with other systemic treatments (control group), while incorporating a study-specific questionnaire to assess feasibility and patient-perceived impact of study procedures. The NTox-PARTICIPATE trial is a single-center prospective pilot study integrating longitudinal neurologic assessments, magnetic resonance imaging, neuromuscular ultrasound, and blood-based immunomonitoring into oncological care. This analysis focuses on patient-reported experiences collected through a study-specific survey assessing satisfaction with study procedures, organizational burden, communication, and the perceived benefit of study participation. Patients were eligible for survey participation after completion of at least 3 study visits. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired ordinal data and the McNemar test for paired binary data. Of 75 enrolled patients, 56 received the survey based on the eligibility criteria and 50 returned completed questionnaires. Patients reported high satisfaction with organizational aspects, communication, response times, counseling on premorbidities and new neurologic conditions, as well as interdisciplinary collaboration (medians +3; 25th percentile +1 or +2, 75th percentile +3). In total, 94% of participants reported increased awareness of newly occurring neurologic symptoms. Notably, 74% of participants perceived an improvement in quality of life through study participation, and 94% expressed willingness to participate again and to recommend the study to others. Longitudinal neurologic monitoring within the NTox-PARTICIPATE framework was feasible and well accepted by patients with cancer. Despite additional organizational effort, patients reported high satisfaction, increased awareness of neurologic symptoms, and improved perceived quality of care attributed to study participation. Integrating patient perspectives alongside structured neurologic assessments may support earlier detection of neurotoxicity, individualized management strategies, and future patient-centered trial design. The study is registered at German Register of Clinical Trials under the identification number DRKS00032520. The approval number of the ethics committee for this study is 2023-3023-BO.

items.title: Hepatitis B and C in Prison: Exploring Prevalence, Prevention and Treatment Needs, and Willingness to Receive Vaccination in Italy.
items.abstract: This study investigated the prevalence of HBV and HCV, HBV vaccination needs, and willingness to undergo HBV vaccination in people in prison in Italy. A cross-sectional study was conducted (October 2023-March 2024) in three prisons in Southern Italy selected to ensure heterogeneity in terms of population and detention characteristics. New arrivals who were expected to remain at the facility for at least 10 days and subjects already present in the facility were eligible. Participants underwent a face-to-face interview, testing for HBV serological markers (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), and anti-HCV screening using a rapid qualitative test. Current HBV infection was defined as HBsAg positivity, past HBV exposure as anti-HBc positivity with or without anti-HBs positivity, HBV vaccine-induced immunity as isolated anti-HBs positivity, and HCV infection as anti-HCV and HCV-RNA positivity.693 PLP were interviewed and screened for HBV and HCV markers. The prevalence of HBV infections was 2.2%, while 15.6% subjects showed past exposure. HBV infection was significantly higher in those aged 41-50 years (OR = 13.49, 95% CI = 1.62-111.9), whereas it was significantly less likely in Italian incarcerated people (OR = 0.07, 95% CI = 0.02-0.3) and those involved in working activities in prison (OR = 0.19, 95% CI = 0.04-0.97). Only 22.1% were immunized through vaccination, and 60.2% were susceptible to infection. Willingness to receive the HBV vaccine in prison was 40.6% and significantly higher in those with longer detention (OR = 2.69, 95% CI = 1.48-4.89) and who attended day hospital (OR = 1.81, 95% CI = 1.01-3.24). The prevalence of HCV was 3.9%, with almost all HCV positive subjects reporting to receive treatment. HCV infection was significantly more likely in older detained people (OR = 4.32, 95% CI = 1.11-16.78), who reported lifetime drug use (OR = 6.89, 95% CI = 1.49-31.91) and intravenous drug use (OR = 8.23, 95% CI = 3.01-22.49), whereas it was less likely in those experiencing their first detention (OR = 0.17, 95% CI = 0.04-0.76). HBV and HCV still circulate among people in prison at higher rates than the general population. Moreover, HBV and HCV screening, as well as HBV vaccination, are not provided to people in prison on a systematic basis. Integrated, multimodal strategies should be adopted to promote opt-out HBV and HCV screening in people in prison and ensure subsequent HBV vaccination or appropriate treatment.

items.title: Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid soluble interleukin-2 receptor α as a biomarker for autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytopathy.
items.abstract: Autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy (GFAP-A) has several proposed biomarkers, but few are readily available in routine practice. This single-center retrospective case-control study evaluated CSF soluble IL-2R α (sIL-2R), a readily measurable marker of T-cell activation, as a clinically accessible marker reflecting CNS inflammatory activity in GFAP-A in the context of autoimmune encephalitis (AE). CSF sIL-2R-related parameters were measured in patients with GFAP-A, MOGAD with encephalitis, anti-NMDAR encephalitis, anti-LGI1 encephalitis, and non-inflammatory neurological diseases (NINDs). sIL-2R was measured using chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay. CSF, CSF/serum sIL-2R quotient (Q sIL-2R ), sIL-2R index (Q sIL-2R /Q albumin ), and Q albumin were compared across the groups, and longitudinal changes were examined. CSF sIL-2R, Q sIL-2R , sIL-2R index, and Q albumin levels were elevated in patients with GFAP-A compared with those in patients with NINDs and other AE groups. CSF sIL-2R discriminated GFAP-A from other selected AE subtypes. CSF predominance of sIL-2R levels was characteristic of GFAP-A. In GFAP-A, sIL-2R quotient diagrams showed Q sIL-2R elevations disproportionate to Q albumin and CSF sIL-2R levels decreased following immunotherapy alongside clinical improvements. These findings suggest that CSF sIL-2R may complement existing biomarkers by supporting the identification of GFAP-A among patients with suspected AE after exclusion of mimics and by providing adjunctive information on treatment-responsive immune activity in GFAP-A.

items.title: Ge/HA scaffolds coupled to XCL-1 induce the migration of immature cDC1.
items.abstract: IntroductionTissue injuries typically trigger an inflammatory response, and scaffolds, hydrogels, and membranes have been developed to treat them; however, a common drawback is the emergence of foreign-body reaction cells, which exacerbate inflammation at the injury site. Scaffolds of gelatin (Ge) and hyaluronic acid (HA) have been used to treat tissue injuries; nevertheless, they must be functionalized with molecules that induce the migration of cells capable of clearing cellular debris, stimulating extracellular matrix production, and maintaining an anti-inflammatory environment-such as conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1). The chemokine XCL-1 is one such molecule known to induce cDC1 migration.ObjectiveThis study aimed to construct a Ge/HA scaffold coupled with XCL-1 to induce the migration of cDC1 with an immature phenotype to induce an anti-inflammatory environment and tissue injury healing.MethodWe fabricated Ge/HA scaffolds with varying concentrations of XCL-1, and the cytotoxicity and cDC1 migration in splenocyte cultures were analyzed. Also, the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on cDC1 that migrated to the scaffolds in both in vivo and in vitro assays. To evaluate the scaffolds' effect in an inflammatory environment, we conjugated them with XCL-1 and IFN-I. We also performed degradation and swelling assays on the XCL-1- and IFN-I-conjugated scaffolds.ConclusionsAll Ge/HA scaffolds were conjugated with XCL-1; however, scaffolds coupled with 100ng/ml of XCL-1 induced the most efficient cDC1 migration both in vivo and in vitro. The cDC1 exhibited a semi-mature phenotype-termed "homeostatic late-mature DC"-implicated in the development of immunological tolerance and the induction of extracellular matrix production. Furthermore, the scaffolds showed low degradation, a high swelling rate, and the constant release of XCL-1 into the extracellular medium-properties that facilitated cDC1 migration. In conclusion, the results suggest that the developed scaffold could be used to treat tissue injuries.

items.title: LINC01136 Facilitates the Progression of HBV-Related Hepatocellular Carcinoma by Regulating the miR-140-5p/JAG1 Axis.
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents highly aggressive tumor with poor prognosis, and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection constitutes its primary etiological factor. To investigate the expression profiles, biological functions, and molecular regulatory mechanisms of long non-coding RNA LINC01136 in HBV-associated HCC (HBV-HCC), and to elucidate the role of the LINC01136/miR-140-5p/JAG1 axis in the malignant progression of HBV-HCC. Clinically, 130 HBV-HCC samples were collected to analyze the association between LINC01136 expression and clinicopathological parameters, as well as prognosis. Cellular functional assays, dual-luciferase reporter assays, RIP assays, and rescue assays were employed to validate the molecular targeting and regulatory relationships. LINC01136 is overexpressed in HBV-HCC tissues and cells and acts as an independent risk predictor for patient prognosis. Knockdown of LINC01136 inhibits malignant behaviors and promotes apoptosis in HCC cells. Mechanistically, LINC01136 functions as a ceRNA for miR-140-5p, thereby upregulating the downstream gene JAG1 and driving HBV-HCC progression. LINC01136 drives HBV-HCC progression via the miR-140-5p/JAG1 pathway, positioning it as a promising biomarker for predicting patient outcome and a potential therapeutic target.

items.title: Real-World Clinical Data-Driven Modeling Reveals Kinetic Concordance Between ALT/HBsAg Ratio and HBsAg Seroclearance in Chronic HBV Infection Patients.
items.abstract: ALT/HBsAg ratio has been proposed as a predictor of HBsAg seroclearance in chronic HBV infection patients, yet its relationship to the underlying within-host kinetics of HBsAg clearance remains undefined. Using a public longitudinal cohort of 1,131 patients and a dual model coupling HBV DNA and HBsAg apparent kinetics, we enrolled 277 patients with ideal HBsAg response within 12 weeks to estimate the apparent HBsAg clearance rate. Among them, 46 patients with biphasic HBV DNA decline were used to estimate the apparent HBV virions clearance rate, and of these, 16 HBeAg-positive patients were used for exploratory estimation of other apparent parameters. Association between these apparent parameters and the ALT/HBsAg ratio were analyzed. Median apparent half-lives were 1.16 days (range: 0.26-8.54) for HBV virions, 15.64 days (range: 1.70-80.31) for HBsAg, and 21.39 days (range: 3.09-219.78) for infected hepatocytes. Higher baseline ALT/HBsAg (HR: 1.009, 95% CI: 1.003-1.014) and higher apparent HBsAg clearance rate (adjusted HR: 1.090, 95% CI: 1.066-1.115) were independently associated with optimal response, with almost identical predicted survival functions. Significantly higher HBsAg apparent clearance rates were observed in HBeAg-negative patients and those with low-level viremia, higher ALT/HBsAg ratios, and achieving optimal response. An inverted V-shaped pattern was identified in HBsAg stratification. This discovery-phase study finds that the ALT/HBsAg ratio is closely associated with model-derived apparent HBsAg clearance kinetics and is concordant with treatment outcome, providing a kinetic interpretation for its clinical predictive relevance.

items.title: Trends in Lyme disease incidence in England, 2013 to 2024.
items.abstract: Official Lyme disease incidence figures for England are based on the number of cases with a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis from the national reference laboratory. However, these figures underestimate the true incidence of acute cases since patients can also be diagnosed clinically without the need for laboratory testing. The use of a multiplication factor has been proposed to estimate total Lyme disease incidence from the number of laboratory-confirmed cases. The current multiplication factor is derived from data spanning 1998-2016 and is thought to be outdated, in part due to the introduction of new national Lyme disease management guidance in 2018. The aim of this study was to analyse more recent laboratory and primary care data to identify trends in case numbers and to derive updated estimates of the total annual number of acute Lyme disease cases in England. Data spanning 2013-2024 from the national reference laboratory and a primary care data source were analysed using seasonal time series models. The presence of structural breaks was investigated using the PELT or BinSeg methods, and annual multiplication factors were estimated using a Poisson regression model. No substantial change was found in the number of laboratory-confirmed Lyme cases from 2013 to 2024 in England, whereas the number of cases diagnosed in primary care increased significantly over the same period, with an average of an additional 498 cases per year. This has increased our best estimate of the multiplication factor from 2.35 (95% confidence interval, 1.81-2.88) to 6.20 (6.17-6.24), which is the average for the years 2020-2024. Use of this updated multiplication factor should improve the accuracy of annual symptomatic Lyme disease case estimates for England.

items.title: Tumor cells incapable of using ketone bodies can still grow in vivo if highly glycolytic.
items.abstract: There has been increasing interest in the potential efficacy of a ketogenic diet in the treatment of cancer. One of the proposed rationales for this is that cancer cells, unlike normal cells, lack the ketolytic enzymes required to utilize ketone bodies for energy, causing selective death to cancer cells under low glucose conditions. In this study, we asked whether cancer cells uniformly lack ketolytic enzymes and whether this correlated with their ability to utilize ketone bodies for survival under low-glucose conditions. In addition, we determined if these in vitro assays could predict the efficacy of a ketogenic diet in vivo using preclinical mouse models. We screened multiple cancer cell lines for their expression of 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1 (OXCT1) and β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), and evaluated their survival under β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB)-supplemented glucose free conditions. We also determined the extent by which βHB is depleted in the cell culture media. The expression of OXCT1 and BDH1 varies between cancer cell lines, and did not always correspond to functional ketone utilization. Furthermore, when tested in vivo using tumor-implanted mouse models, many cancer cells grew regardless of their predicted ketolytic capacity, highlighting the limited ability of these in vitro findings to predict in vivo efficacy. The growth of SW480 colon cancer cells, shown in vitro to be a user of βHB, was slowed to a greater extent when implanted in vivo to mice fed a ketogenic diet, when compared to H1299 lung cancer cells, which were not a user of βHB in vitro. Further investigations suggest that H1299 is a greater producer of lactate, which we hypothesize is being converted back to glucose in the liver via gluconeogenesis, causing the observed higher blood glucose and plasma insulin. This in turn, supports the growth of the H1299 cells in vivo, that could not be predicted by our in vitro assays. Taken together, we show that while it is not possible to predict the efficacy of a ketogenic diet using in vitro assays, it may be possible to identify which cancer cells may be impacted under low glucose conditions based on its propensity to produce lactate via glycolysis.

items.title: Associated comorbidities among people living with HIV: A retrospective matched cohort study in Spain.
items.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (PLWH) have more comorbidities and higher mortality than their non-HIV counterparts, in spite of their improving survival. This study aimed to: 1) characterize a cohort of PLWH using real-world data from the public health system users in Aragon region, Spain; 2) compare the prevalence of specific long-term conditions between PLWH and a matched cohort of people not living with HIV (PNLWH); 3) determine the association between HIV infection and these conditions, controlling for key confounders (sex, year of birth, geographic area, socioeconomic status, and country of birth); and 4) determine whether PLWH are diagnosed with other new comorbidities earlier than PNLWH. Retrospective observational matched cohort study of 8,302 PLWH matched 1:2 in Aragon, Spain. PLWH had higher multimorbidity burden (median 2 (interquartile range 1, 5) vs 2 (0, 4), increasing with age especially in women, and experienced approximately twice the mortality observed among PNLWH (20,8% in PLWH vs 8,6% in PNLWH). Mental health problems, cardiovascular events, neoplasms and hepatic diseases were more common in PLWH, and these conditions were recorded earlier compared with PNLWH. In men LWH under 45 years, depression showed an adjusted odds ratio (OR) of 2.23 (1.73-2.88). In women LWH aged 45-65 years, congestive heart failure showed an adjusted OR of 60.9 (8.70-426.06). They tended to be diagnosed less frequently with classic cardiovascular risk factors like obesity, or dyslipidemia (OR 0.74 [0.67-0.83] in males aged 45-65 years). PLWH experienced a higher burden of morbidity and approximately twice the mortality rate of PNLWH. They were also diagnosed with new chronic conditions at an earlier age than PNLWH. Although PLWH had a higher incidence of cardiovascular events, they had fewer recorded diagnoses of certain cardiovascular risk factors. The existence of different comorbidity profiles in both cohorts shows us that further investigation is needed to assess the influence of HIV infection with respect to the diagnosis and management of comorbidities.

items.title: Histopathological and Transcriptomic Features of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-related T-cell-mediated Rejection in Liver Transplantation.
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related T-cell-mediated rejection (irTCMR) leads to greater steroid resistance and graft loss compared with conventional T-cell-mediated rejection (cTCMR) in liver transplant recipients. However, their histopathological and transcriptomic features remain poorly understood. Thirty-one adult recipients with biopsy-proven T-cell-mediated rejection (12 irTCMR and 19 cTCMR) were enrolled. Biopsies were assessed using the Banff and Ishak scoring systems, with immunohistochemical staining for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, programmed death-ligand 1, and C4d. Spatial transcriptomic analysis was performed on the CD45-enriched portal areas. irTCMR showed higher alanine aminotransferase/aspartate aminotransferase peaks, steroid-resistant rejection (33.3% versus 0%; P = 0.016), and graft loss (41.7% versus 0%; P = 0.005). IrTCMR had a higher rejection activity index (median 6 versus 5; P = 0.020), driven by more severe bile duct inflammation and venous endothelialitis. Ishak scoring revealed a higher histological activity index with greater confluent necrosis (P = 0.046). Both groups showed CD8+ predominant T-cell aggregates with sparse CD20+ B cells; CD4+ abundance (P = 0.079) and the CD4/CD8 ratio (P = 0.096) tended to be higher in irTCMR. Portal C4d deposition and programmed death-ligand 1 expression showed no significant differences. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct transcriptomic profiles in irTCMR, with 75 differentially expressed genes and enrichment of allograft rejection and antigen processing pathways. Immune deconvolution demonstrated increased CD4+ T cells, dendritic cells, and M1 macrophages but reduced regulatory T cells in irTCMR. irTCMR is a distinct aggressive rejection phenotype with severe bile duct inflammation, venous endothelialitis, confluent necrosis, and transcriptomic features distinct from cTCMR. These features underscore the need for further research on the pathogenesis of irTCMR.
